extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners handling design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination of U.S. design patent applications, including handling of restriction traversals, double patenting (statutory and nonstatutory), priority claims under 35 U.S.C. §§119/120, and continuation/CIP practice. Focused on examiner procedures and applicant requirements for entitlement and rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traversal of restriction requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a response to a restriction requirement includes an election with traverse on the grounds that the groups are not patentably distinct, applicant must present evidence or identify such evidence of record showing the groups to be obvious variations of one another. Traversal of a restriction requirement alone without an explanation in support thereof will be treated as an election without traverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must present evidence or point to evidence of record; mere assertion is insufficient. See MPEP §818.03(a) and form paragraph 8.25.02. Note: an argument that there is 'no serious burden' to search the entire application (MPEP §803) is not applicable to design patent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner response to a traversal
rubrics_metrics.description: When a traversal specifically points out the supposed errors in a restriction, examiners must reevaluate the requirement in view of these remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If restriction is to be maintained it must be repeated and made final in the next Office action and the arguments answered. No application should be allowed on the next Office action where a response includes an election with traverse, unless the traversal is withdrawn in view of a telephone interview, or the examiner withdraws the restriction requirement. See MPEP §821.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of double patenting rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: There are generally two types of double patenting rejections: (1) the 'same invention' type based on 35 U.S.C. 171 and (2) the 'nonstatutory-type' double patenting rejection (judicially created) intended primarily to prevent prolongation of patent term by prohibiting claims not patentably distinct from claims in a first patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPEP §804 charts for procedure. Double patenting rejections are based on comparison of claims; the disclosure may be relied upon only to define the claim. Determine whether the same design is claimed twice (statutory) or whether designs are patentably indistinct variations of the same inventive concept (nonstatutory).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Same invention" double patenting (35 U.S.C. 171)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design-design statutory double patenting rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 prevents the issuance of a second patent for a design already patented. For this type to be proper, identical designs with identical scope must be twice claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'same invention' type cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer. Use form paragraph 15.23 (and 15.23.02 summary). Apply when the same design is being claimed twice (compare claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design-utility "same invention" double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: A design-utility 'same invention' double patenting rejection is based on judicial doctrine (no statutory basis) when the same invention is claimed in a design and a utility patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine is applied as in In re Thorington. The 'same invention' type (statutory or nonstatutory) cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer (In re Swett). Use appropriate form paragraphs 15.24.07/15.24.08 where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory (obviousness-type) double patenting general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonstatutory double patenting rejection is based on a judicially created doctrine grounded in public policy to prevent unjustified timewise extension of the right to exclude. It applies where claims are directed to the same inventive concept with different appearances or differing scope which are patentably indistinct from each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be overcome by submission of a terminal disclaimer (subject to ownership/common ownership conditions). Precede such rejections with form paragraph 15.24.06 (heading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case for obviousness-type double patenting (designs)
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness-type double patenting: (A) the conflicting design claims must have overall appearances with basically the same design characteristics; and (B) the differences between the two designs must be insufficient to patentably distinguish one design from the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim in the reference must be considered as a whole (overall appearance), not by isolated elements. Differences may be considered patentably insufficient when they are de minimis or obvious to a designer of ordinary skill in the art. Perform the factual inquiries under Graham v. John Deere and then determine if results support a prima facie obviousness-type double patenting conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type double patenting when designs have differing scope (A–C test)
rubrics_metrics.description: When designs have differing scope, a rejection is appropriate if: (A) the difference in scope is minor and patentably indistinct; (B) patent protection for the design, fully disclosed in and covered by the claim of the reference, would be extended by allowance of the later claim; and (C) no terminal disclaimer has been filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider combination vs subcombination (narrow vs broad claim). If the narrower claim is not fully disclosed in the broader reference, a nonstatutory double patenting rejection is inappropriate. Additional disclosure may be in title, descriptive statement, or broken-line drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison limitations between utility and design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting rejections are based on a comparison of claims; while there is a direct correlation between drawings and claim in a design application, no such correlation is necessary in a utility application or patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any double patenting consideration between a utility application/patent and a design application cannot be based on the utility drawing disclosure alone. The examiner must be able to recreate the design claimed from the utility claims without reliance on the drawings. See Anchor Hocking Corp. v. Eyelet Specialty Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional double patenting procedural handling
rubrics_metrics.description: If a provisional double patenting rejection (of any type) is the only rejection remaining in two conflicting applications, the examiner should withdraw that rejection in one application (e.g., the application with the earlier filing date) and permit that application to issue; maintain the provisional rejection in the other application, converting it when the first issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more than two applications conflict and one is allowed, remaining applications should be cross rejected against the others and the allowed application. Ensure common inventorship or assignee conditions are met for such rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership / inventorship requirement for double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: For a double patenting rejection to be appropriate there must be either at least one inventor in common, or a common assignee between the conflicting applications/patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims in copending design applications or a design patent and design applications have a common assignee but different inventive entities, consider rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/(f)/(g) or 103(a) in addition to double patenting. See MPEP §§804, 2136–2138.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer for nonstatutory double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely filed terminal disclaimer in compliance with 37 CFR 1.321(c) may be used to overcome an actual or provisional rejection based on a nonstatutory double patenting ground provided the conflicting application or patent is shown to be commonly owned with this application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 15.24.06 should precede nonstatutory rejections. Effective Jan 1, 1994, registered attorney or agent of record may sign a terminal disclaimer; if signed by assignee, must comply with 37 CFR 3.73(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing rule distinguishing nonstatutory rejection vs prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonstatutory double patenting rejection over a patent should only be given if the patent issued less than a year before the filing date of the application; if the patent is more than a year older, the patent is considered 'prior art' and should be applied under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)/103(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use correct statutory grounds depending on timing of the patent issuance relative to the application filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design obviousness test (Rationale for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejections)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unobviousness in the overall appearance of the claimed design, when compared with the prior art, rather than minute details or small variations in design, that constitutes the test of design patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 15.67 (Rationale for 35 U.S.C. 103(a) Rejection). Cite In re Frick and In re Lamb. Focus on overall appearance rather than isolated features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type double patenting with multiple references
rubrics_metrics.description: When making an obviousness-type double patenting rejection using multiple references, the claim is rejected under the judicially created doctrine of obviousness-type double patenting of the claim(s) in the cited patent(s) in view of secondary references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how at the time applicant made the design it would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill to modify the basic reference as demonstrated by the secondary references, identifying the modifications and the secondary references teaching them. Use form paragraphs 15.24/15.24.04 and 15.68 and cite relevant case law on combining references (In re Rosen, Carter, Glavas, Antle, Nalbandian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of priority for designs under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) (six-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of priority provided by subsections (a) through (d) of section 119 and the time specified in section 102(d) shall be six months in the case of designs. The right of priority under section 119(e) shall not apply to designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain benefit of an earlier foreign filing date, the U.S. application must be filed within six months of the earliest foreign filing date for the same design. Design applications may not claim priority to a provisional under 119(e). See MPEP §1504.10 and §15.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and required information for claiming foreign priority (treaties)
rubrics_metrics.description: When claiming priority based on filings under bilateral/multilateral treaties (e.g., Hague Agreement, Benelux, European Community Design), the following information must be supplied in addition to application number and filing date: (A) the name of the treaty under which the application was filed, (B) the name of at least one country other than the U.S. where the application has effect, and (C) the name and location of the national or intergovernmental authority which received the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also supply certified copy of the foreign application papers when required. See MPEP Chapter 200 and 37 CFR 1.55 for procedure. Attention to special requirements when an actual model was originally filed in Germany (MPEP §201.14(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) — certified copy/timing
rubrics_metrics.description: No design patent application is entitled to right of priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(b) unless a claim therefor and a certified copy of the original foreign application, specification and drawings are filed in the USPTO before the issue fee is paid, or at such time during pendency as required by the Director (not earlier than six months after filing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The certification must be made by the foreign patent office or proper authority and show dates. The Director may require translations and other information as necessary. See MPEP §15.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of prior U.S. application(s) when claiming benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant is entitled under 35 U.S.C. 120 to the benefit of an earlier U.S. filing date, the statement such as 'This is a division [continuation] of design Application No. ———, filed ———.' should appear in the first sentence(s) of the specification (or be included in an application data sheet per 37 CFR 1.76).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR 1.78(a)(2) requires this; failure to timely submit such a reference is considered a waiver of benefit. Form paragraph 15.26 may be used to remind applicant and a suggested format is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement for entitlement to benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are entitled to claim the benefit of earlier applications under 35 U.S.C. 120 only when the earlier application discloses the invention in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In continuation and divisional applications, the examiner must determine whether conditions for priority under 120 have been met. If the claimed design in a continuation/divisional is not disclosed in the original application, the later application is not entitled to benefit and examiner should notify applicant with reasons, using form paragraphs 2.09/2.10 and require cancellation of the 'benefit' statement or submission of a supplemental ADS where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation-in-part (CIP) entitlement and C‑I‑P caution
rubrics_metrics.description: A design application filed as a continuation-in-part to supply deficiencies in the first application is not entitled to the benefit of the earlier filing date if the first application is fatally defective under 35 U.S.C. 112 (written description). A C‑I‑P that changes the shape or configuration of a design disclosed in an earlier application is not entitled to benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 15.74 should be used to notify applicant that a C‑I‑P is not entitled to benefit. If the first application is fatally defective, a later-filed CIP to supply the deficiency will not get the earlier date (Hunt Co. v. Mallinckrodt). However, if the filing date is not actually needed (e.g., not to avoid intervening prior art), the entitlement need not be determined. See In re Corba.

rubrics_metrics.name: C‑I‑P claiming benefit where parent claimed foreign priority — foreign status determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a C‑I‑P claims benefit under 35 U.S.C. 120 to an earlier U.S. application which in turn claims priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) to a foreign application, and the conditions of 120 are not met, the examiner must determine whether the foreign application has matured into a form of patent protection. If it has matured and would anticipate or render the CIP claim obvious, the foreign application qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(d)/172 and the CIP claim should be rejected under 102/103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the charts in MPEP §1504.02 to determine the status of the foreign application. If status cannot be determined, use appropriate form paragraphs (15.75/15.75.01) to explain rejection or caution.
